title: The Sun
tagline: The star that lights and warms everything
description: The Sun isn't a planet — it's a star, a huge ball of super-hot gas that shines with its own light. It sits at the center of the Solar System, and its gravity is what keeps every planet spinning around it.
sizeFact: The Sun is so big that more than a million Earths could fit inside it!
whyFact: Deep inside the Sun, atoms crash into each other so hard that they turn into other atoms and release a huge amount of light and heat — that's what we feel as the Sun's glow.
funFact: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth, even traveling at the speed of light!

title: Mercury
tagline: The closest planet to the Sun
description: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and also the smallest of them all. It's a rocky world covered in craters, a bit like our Moon, with almost no atmosphere to protect it.
sizeFact: Mercury is so small that more than 18 Mercuries could fit inside Earth!
whyLabel: Why is it scorching by day and freezing by night?
whyFact: Since Mercury has almost no atmosphere to trap heat, it gets scorching hot in sunlight during the day and freezing cold at night — the biggest temperature swing of any planet in the Solar System.
funFact: A year on Mercury (one trip around the Sun) takes only 88 Earth days, but a single day on Mercury lasts even longer than that!

title: Venus
tagline: The hottest planet, hidden in clouds
description: Venus is about the same size as Earth, which is why it's sometimes called Earth's "twin planet" — but it's very different. It's covered in thick clouds of a gas that traps heat, making it the hottest planet in the Solar System.
sizeFact: Venus is almost exactly the same size as Earth — the two planets are like size-twins, but very different underneath.
whyLabel: Why is Venus hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun?
whyFact: Venus's thick clouds trap the Sun's heat like a very heavy blanket — this is called the greenhouse effect. That's why Venus ends up hotter than Mercury, even though it's farther from the Sun.
funFact: On Venus, one day (a single spin) actually lasts longer than one whole year (one trip around the Sun)!

title: Earth and the Moon
description: Earth is the only planet we know of with life. It has liquid water, air to breathe, and a balanced temperature — not too hot, not too cold. The Moon is our natural satellite, a ball of rock that circles the Earth.
sizeFact: The Moon is much smaller than Earth — about 4 Moons would fit side by side across Earth's diameter.
whyLabel: Why do we have day and night?
whyFact: Earth is always spinning on itself, like a top. The side facing the Sun has daytime; the side facing away has nighttime. One full spin takes 24 hours.
funFact: The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans and causes the tides!

title: Mars
description: Mars is known as the "red planet" because of the color of its surface. It's smaller than Earth, has two tiny moons, and is the planet scientists study most closely when looking for signs that life may once have existed there.
sizeFact: Mars is much smaller than Earth — almost 7 Marses would fit inside Earth.
whyFact: Mars's soil is full of iron, the same metal found in blood and in nails. When iron is exposed to air, it rusts — and that "rust" gives Mars its reddish-orange color.
funFact: Mars has the biggest volcano in the whole Solar System, Olympus Mons, almost 3 times taller than Mount Everest!

title: Jupiter
tagline: The giant of the Solar System
description: Jupiter is by far the biggest planet in the Solar System. It's a giant ball made mostly of gas, with no solid surface to land on. It has a giant storm called the Great Red Spot, which has been swirling for hundreds of years.
sizeFact: Jupiter is so big that more than 1000 Earths could fit inside it!
whyLabel: Why does the Great Red Spot never go away?
whyFact: The Great Red Spot is a storm so huge — bigger than Earth itself! — that it has kept spinning for hundreds of years, fed by Jupiter's incredibly strong winds.
funFact: Jupiter has more than 90 known moons — it's almost like its own little solar system!

title: Saturn
description: Saturn is famous for its wide, shiny rings, made of millions of pieces of ice and rock, ranging from tiny dust grains to huge chunks. Like Jupiter, it's a gas giant.
sizeFact: Saturn is so light for its size that if you had an ocean big enough, Saturn would float on it!
whyFact: Saturn's rings are made of pieces of ice and rock that got caught circling the planet, held in place by its gravity, instead of joining together into a moon or falling onto the planet.
funFact: Saturn's rings are very wide but incredibly thin — in many places they're only as thick as a small building!

title: Uranus
tagline: The planet that spins "on its side"
description: Uranus is an ice giant, with a blue-green color caused by a gas called methane in its atmosphere. It's different from every other planet because it spins almost lying on its side, like a rolling ball.
sizeFact: Uranus is about 4 times wider than Earth.
whyLabel: Why does Uranus spin "on its side"?
whyFact: Scientists think that a very long time ago, something huge — maybe a planet the size of Earth — crashed into Uranus and knocked it so hard that it has been spinning nearly sideways ever since.
funFact: On Uranus, each pole has a night that lasts about 21 Earth years in a row!

title: Neptune
description: Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun and, like Uranus, an ice giant, with a deep, beautiful blue color. It's an extremely windy world, with the strongest winds ever measured on any planet.
sizeFact: Neptune is so far from the Sun that it takes almost 165 Earth years to go around it once!
whyLabel: Why does Neptune have such strong winds?
whyFact: Neptune gets very little light and heat from the Sun, and the temperature difference between parts of the planet creates ferocious winds that can blow at more than 2000 km/h.
funFact: Since it was discovered in 1846, Neptune has only completed one full orbit of the Sun, finishing it in 2011!

title: Pluto and the Dwarf Planets
description: Pluto used to be called the 9th planet, but today scientists call it a "dwarf planet" because it's small and shares its region of space with many similar objects, like Eris, Ceres, and Haumea.
sizeFact: Pluto is so small it would fit inside Russia if you laid it on top of a map of Earth!
whyLabel: Why did Pluto stop being called a planet?
whyFact: In 2006, scientists set new rules for what counts as a "planet": it must be round, orbit the Sun, and have "cleared" its orbit of other objects. Pluto meets the first two, but not the third — so it became a dwarf planet instead.
funFact: Pluto has a moon almost as big as itself, called Charon — that's why some scientists call them a "double planet"!

title: Asteroids and Comets
tagline: Traveling rocks and balls of ice
description: Besides the planets, the Solar System has millions of chunks of rock (asteroids) and balls of ice and dust (comets) traveling through space. Most asteroids live in a zone between Mars and Jupiter called the asteroid belt.
sizeFact: Most asteroids are small — the size of a rock or a building — but a few are hundreds of kilometers wide!
whyLabel: Why do comets have a bright tail?
whyFact: A comet is like a dirty snowball made of ice and dust. As it gets close to the Sun, the heat melts part of the ice, turning it into gas and dust that the Sun pushes behind it, forming a long, bright tail.
funFact: Asteroids and comets have hit Earth before — one, 66 million years ago, may have helped wipe out the dinosaurs!
